## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nanda Sutta* (Ud 3.2, PTS Ud 21) is a canonical discourse in the *Udāna* collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. In this narrative, the Buddha intervenes when his half-brother Nanda experiences dissatisfaction with the monastic life; the Buddha makes a pact with him, guaranteeing that if he perseveres as a monk, he will be rewarded with celestial nymphs in his next life [SuttaCentral]. The text is also explicitly referenced in later Pali literature in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.3.3, *Vatthaguyhanidassanapañha*) [SuttaCentral].

SuttaCentral identifies verse parallels to the sutta in the Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga* traditions (UV 32, UVS 32, and Uv Kg 32, *Bhikṣuvarga*) and the Chinese recension of the *Dharmapada*/*Udānavarga* (*Fa ji yao song jing*, T 213.32), alongside a resembling narrative discourse in the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EA 18.7) [SuttaCentral]. In automated text-reuse analyses by DharmaNexus, the discourse shares passages with 108 Pali texts [DharmaNexus]. Its largest Pali reuse partner is the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* (§11.1–15.1), which recounts the story of Nanda, alongside extensive prose formula reuse across the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 5, AN 6, AN 8, AN 3, AN 10), the *Dīgha Nikāya* (DN 16), and various saṁyuttas of the *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 35, SN 22, SN 55, SN 7, SN 16, SN 6, SN 1) [DharmaNexus]. Across languages, DharmaNexus aligns segments of the text with Chinese translations, including the *Ekottarika-āgama* (T 125, fascicle 9, plausibility score 95), consistent with the parallel listed by SuttaCentral, as well as matches with the *Saṁyukta-āgama* (T 99, T 100) and Tibetan canonical texts [DharmaNexus]. None of the sampled reference passages directly discuss Ud 3.2, reflecting homonymous matches with unrelated texts.

*No discussion of this text was found in the reference-literature corpus; the overview relies on SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus data.*
